idiom_name: function-pointer validator with an explicit context struct
implementation_notes: C has no generics and no typeclass layer, so the pattern collapses to a struct holding a function pointer plus whatever state the check needs - struct validator { bool (*fn)(void *ctx, const void *value); void *ctx; } - and the combinators are adapter functions that re-enter two validators. divide is emulated by projecting the input to a sub-struct or field and running a component validator on it; choose is a switch on a tag field that re-dispatches; conquer is a function that returns true. The classic structure pays off when the same check is shared across call sites (a comparator for qsort/bsearch, a filter callback, a table of field checks); a single call site keeps the plain if.
pitfalls: Type safety is gone at the boundary: void * payloads make an int * versus int64_t * mix-up a silent memory bug - keep the cast in one adapter per concrete type and never reuse a validator across element sizes.
Context lifetime is manual: a validator whose ctx points to freed or stack-allocated configuration reads garbage; store contexts with the same lifetime as the validator and document who owns them.
A boolean verdict discards the reason, so a composed check must also return an error index (or write into an out-parameter) when callers need to report more than 'no'.
